This is not a real conflict — it is the same event recorded twice using two different year-start conventions, and once you see that, the "disagreement" dissolves entirely.

## What is happening

England used the **Old Style (Julian) calendar** until the Calendar (New Style) Act 1750 took effect on **1 January 1752**. Under Old Style reckoning, the legal year began on **25 March** (Lady Day), not 1 January.

14 February falls *between* 1 January and 24 March — the ambiguous window where the historical year and the civil year diverged:

| Convention | Year start | How 14 Feb is written | Describes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Old Style (register) | 25 March | 14 Feb **1746** | Same day |
| New Style (transcript) | 1 January | 14 Feb **1747** | Same day |

The Bolton-le-Moors parish register used Old Style — standard for Anglican registers of that era. The printed transcript silently converted to New Style by advancing the year by one for any date before 25 March. Both sources are describing **the same baptism on the same day**.

## Which year to record

Use the **double-dated form: 14 February 1746/47**. This is the scholarly standard (Evidence Explained §2.36) because it:
- Faithfully represents what the register says (1746)
- Signals to every reader that the modern equivalent is 1747
- Eliminates exactly the confusion you just encountered

If your software forces a single year, use **1747 NS** (New Style) and add a source note explaining the register reads "1746 OS."

## Handling a_001 and a_002

There is no evidentiary conflict to resolve between these two assertions — they carry identical information. What you *do* have is a **derivative source problem**: the printed transcript introduced a conversion without flagging it, which is a known hazard of published register abstracts. Record the register (a_001) as the authoritative assertion at 1746/47, note that a_002 is a derivative that silently modernised the year, and classify a_002's 1747 date as *derived* rather than independently corroborating.

fields.resolution_rationale:
The question is whether the Patrick Flynn in the 1870 Allegheny County census (a_014) is the same man as subject I1, documented in Schuylkill County. The answer determines which records belong to this research target and whether the subject's life between 1860 and 1908 included a long-distance relocation.

The 1870 Allegheny County census (src_005) records a Patrick Flynn as head of household. The enumerator visited the dwelling directly, making this a reliable record of where that man lived. His name and age (consistent with ca. 1845 birth) match the subject. On the other side, three independent records anchor the subject to Schuylkill County: (a) the 1850 census placing Patrick Flynn, age ~5, in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household (src_001); (b) the 1860 census placing him at age ~15 in the same household (src_003); and (c) the 1908 death certificate, with son-in-law James Brown reporting the subject's death in Schuylkill County (src_004).

The preponderance favors the Allegheny County record belonging to a distinct individual. Three independent records from different enumerators and informants anchor the subject to Schuylkill County across 58 years. The Allegheny entry is a single uncorroborated record. If it were the subject, he would have moved 320 km west — with no surviving bridge record — and returned 320 km east by 1908, again undocumented. Moreover, 'Patrick Flynn' ranked among the most common Irish-American names in Pennsylvania's industrial counties; both the Schuylkill anthracite region and Allegheny County's Pittsburgh corridor drew heavily from the same Irish emigrant stream, producing large communities where this name appeared abundantly.

The most defensible explanation is a same-name disambiguation problem well-documented in Pennsylvania industrial-county records: a separate Patrick Flynn, part of the distinct Irish immigrant community working in Pittsburgh-area iron and steel, was enumerated in Allegheny County in 1870. This is not the subject. The conflict remains unresolved — not because evidence is equal on both sides, but because a 'different persons' finding affords no preferred assertion under the schema. Decisive records would include: (1) an 1870 census entry placing the subject in Schuylkill County, definitively excluding the Allegheny record; (2) an 1880 census for the Allegheny County Patrick Flynn confirming continued Pittsburgh-area residence as a distinct person; or (3) a marriage record or city directory entry for either man firmly establishing county residence ca. 1865–1880.

Let me read the project state and assertions before doing anything else.

Good. Now let me fetch Norway's naming customs — required before handling any patronymic question.

I have everything I need. The naming customs page confirms Norway was fully in its patronymic era in 1875 — the decisive fact here. Let me now create the conflict entry and complete the full analysis.

Good. Now I'll update with the full independence analysis, weighing analysis, and resolution rationale in one write.

**c_001 written — status: `unresolved`**

**The conflict:** The 1875 Ringsaker census names the principal "Anders Pedersen," but the research subject is Anders Hansen, son of Hans Olsen. Age (~7) and district match; the patronymic does not.

**Decisive finding — patronymic mismatch in an active system.** Norway's naming customs wiki confirms the country was fully in its patronymic era in 1875 (the first name law wasn't passed until 1923). "Pedersen" encodes *son of Peder*; a son of Hans Olsen would be "Hansen." These are not spelling variants — they encode different fathers. The household informant who gave the child's name to the enumerator would have known the father firsthand. Two boys named Anders, both ~7, in the same rural district is entirely plausible given traditional Norwegian naming patterns; the surface match is not enough to overcome the patronymic signal.

**Why it stays `unresolved`:** The analysis concludes *different persons*, which means no assertion among the competing set represents our subject — the schema requires a `preferred_assertion_id` from the competing set for a `resolved` status, and none qualifies here.

---

**What would decide it — three decisive record types:**

1. **The census household image itself** — if the head of household for "Anders Pedersen" in the 1875 enumeration is named *Peder* (not Hans), that proves two distinct families and closes the question.
2. **A second 1875 census entry** — finding Anders Hansen in a Ringsaker household headed by Hans Olsen would positively place your subject and confirm the census persona is someone else.
3. **The Ringsaker baptism register** — a parish baptism entry naming both parents would settle the father's given name beyond any doubt.

Would you like me to create a research question targeting those records (question-selection), or go straight to searching the 1875 census image to check the household head (search-images)?

fields.weighing_analysis: The decisive factor is the patronymic. The FamilySearch Norway Naming Customs wiki confirms that most of Norway's population used patronymic surnames derived from the father's given name throughout the 19th century; the first name law was not passed until 1923. In 1875 Ringsaker, 'Pedersen' unambiguously encodes 'son of Peder.' The research subject's known father is Hans Olsen, whose son would bear the patronymic 'Hansen' — son of Hans. 'Pedersen' and 'Hansen' encode different fathers and are not spelling variants of each other in any standard or dialectal form. The household member who reported to the enumerator would have known the father's name firsthand, making this a proximate, primary report. The matching given name (Anders), estimated birth year (~1868), and district (Ringsaker, Hedmark) are consistent — but these surface features are insufficient to overcome the patronymic signal: traditional Norwegian naming patterns (first son named for paternal grandfather) made Anders a very common given name, and two boys of similar age with the same given name in the same rural district is historically plausible. No evidence in the project establishes that Hans Olsen was ever known as or called Peder, and the project objective itself records the father as 'Hans Olsen.'
fields.resolution_rationale: The conflict concerns whether the 1875 census persona 'Anders Pedersen' (assertions a_001–a_002) is the research subject Anders Hansen, son of Hans Olsen. The surface match — same given name, same approximate age (~7), same district — prompted the hit, but the patronymic is irreconcilable. Norway was fully within its patronymic era in 1875: a son of Hans Olsen would be recorded as Hansen, not Pedersen. The census enumerator was recording what a household member stated; that informant would have known the child's father firsthand. The patronymic 'Pedersen' therefore names a different father — Peder, not Hans — and the skill instruction is explicit: a patronymic mismatch in an active patronymic system is a different-person signal, never a spelling variant. The preponderance of evidence indicates these are two distinct boys: the census 'Anders Pedersen' (son of a Peder) and the research subject Anders Hansen (son of Hans Olsen). Because the conclusion is 'different persons,' there is no assertion in the competing set that represents our subject, so no preferred_assertion_id can be named and status remains unresolved. What would confirm this conclusively: (1) identify the head of household for 'Anders Pedersen' in the 1875 census image — if that man is named Peder (not Hans), the distinction is proved; (2) locate a separate 1875 Ringsaker census entry for Anders Hansen in a household headed by Hans Olsen; (3) obtain the baptism register entry for the subject from Ringsaker parish records, which would name both parents and settle the father's given name beyond doubt.
